title: Policies to control inflation and deflation

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Set out the range of policies against inflation and deflation, and weigh how effective each is likely to be.

blocks.heading: The range of policies
blocks.text: Against inflation a government and its central bank hold three routes. Monetary policy: raising interest rates makes borrowing dearer and saving better rewarded, slowing the growth of total spending. Fiscal policy: cutting government spending or raising taxes removes spending from the economy directly. Supply-side measures that raise capacity or ease input costs - infrastructure, training, cheaper logistics - work on cost pressure where spending restraint cannot. Against deflation the routes run in reverse: interest rates are cut and government spending climbs, aimed at restarting total spending before the chains of the last section take hold.

blocks.heading: A rate rise against demand-pull pressure
blocks.text: Suppose the central bank lifts its policy rate from 5% to 9% against a 6% yearly climb in prices driven by fast credit growth. Loans become dearer, so households borrow less and firms postpone loan-financed expansion, and saving is better rewarded, so the economy's whole outlay grows more slowly. With sellers no longer able to count on buyers bidding against each other, the demand-pull pressure eases. Consumers face gentler price moves and savers gain income, while borrowers meet dearer credit and firms weaker sales while the policy works.

blocks.heading: How effective each route is
blocks.text: Effectiveness depends on the cause of the climb. Where outlay runs ahead of capacity, the rate rise is well aimed and works through the whole banking system at once. Where costs push prices up - a fuel rise, a poor harvest - dearer borrowing squeezes output and jobs without touching the cause, and supply-side measures or waiting out the input price do more. The effects also arrive with a delay, and deflation is harder still: households expecting lower prices may keep postponing even with cheap credit, where confidence is low. Each route trades against other aims - slower growth and fewer jobs while prices come down, or higher public borrowing where the government spends against deflation.

blocks.heading: Fighting deflation, and how well it works
blocks.text: Against deflation the routes run in reverse, and how well they work depends on the cause and on confidence. Where deflation comes from the demand side, the central bank cuts interest rates, so borrowing is cheaper and saving pays less, encouraging households and firms to spend now; and the government raises its own spending or cuts taxes, adding orders directly or leaving households more income to spend. Because a demand-side fall leaves factories idle and workers without jobs, there is spare capacity, so extra spending tends to raise output and employment, and rising incomes add further spending - the reverse of the chain in the last section. The limits are real. Where households expect prices to keep falling, they may keep postponing purchases even when credit is cheap. Once interest rates are close to zero there is little room to cut further. And extra government spending adds to public borrowing that later taxpayers repay. Japan shows the difficulty: prices drifted down for long stretches from the late 1990s even though its interest rates were held close to zero. Where deflation comes from the supply side - cheaper inputs or higher productivity, with output holding - there may be little to cure, because jobs and output are not falling, and a government may choose to leave it alone.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The interest-rate route is topic 4.4, the spending-and-taxation route topic 4.3, and both serve the aims of topic 4.2.
